diagnosis_explanation:
# Your Lung Condition

You have a lung disease called COPD. Your lungs have trouble moving air in and out. Right now, your condition got worse. That is called an exacerbation.

COPD happens over many years. Smoking or air pollution can cause it. Your lungs get more and more scarred. The airways get narrow and tight.

When you have an exacerbation, your symptoms get much worse. You may cough more. You may feel short of breath. You may feel tired.

The hospital treated you for this flare-up. Now you need to keep taking care of your lungs at home.

---

# Your Other Health Conditions

**Your Heart Rhythm:**
Your heart sometimes beats in an odd way. This is called atrial fibrillation. Your doctors are watching this. The medicines you take help keep it steady.

**Your Weight:**
Your weight is higher than is best for your health. Extra weight makes it harder for your heart and lungs to work. Losing even a small amount can help you feel better.

**Your Blood Pressure:**
Your blood pressure is higher than normal. This puts extra work on your heart.

**Your Blood Sugar:**
You have Type 2 Diabetes. Your blood sugar is higher than it should be. This can affect many parts of your body over time.

All of these conditions are linked. Taking care of one helps the others too.
medication_rationale:
Tiotropium:
This medicine keeps your lungs open all day and night. It helps you breathe easier by relaxing the muscles around your airways. You use it once a day with a special device called a Handihaler. Use it even when you feel fine. Your breathing should feel a bit easier each day.

Formoterol/Budesonide:
This is a two-in-one medicine for your lungs. It opens your airways and reduces swelling inside them. You take two puffs twice a day, even when feeling okay. Rinse your mouth with water after each use. This helps prevent mouth infections. Your chest may feel less tight over the next few days.

Albuterol:
Use this medicine when you feel short of breath or tight in the chest. It opens your airways very fast, usually within minutes. Take two puffs and wait a few minutes. You can use it every four to six hours as needed. If you need this more than three times a week, tell your doctor.

Prednisone:
This strong medicine reduces the swelling in your lungs caused by your flare-up. Start with 40 mg once a day for five days. Then drop to 30 mg once a day for five days. Then drop to 20 mg once a day for five days. Follow this exact schedule your doctor gave you. You may feel hungrier or have trouble sleeping. This is normal with this medicine. You may also feel your mood change a bit. These side effects go away when you finish the medicine. Call your doctor if you feel very shaky, very confused, or have a high fever.
Important: Do not stop taking this medicine without calling your doctor first.

Digoxin:
This medicine helps control your heart rate. It slows down a heart rhythm problem you have called atrial fibrillation. Take one pill once a day. Your heart should beat at a steadier pace. Tell your doctor right away if your heart feels like it is racing, skipping beats, or fluttering. Also call if you feel very sick to your stomach or throw up a lot.

Metoprolol tartrate:
This medicine helps your heart work better and lowers blood pressure. Take 25 mg twice a day. You may feel a bit tired or slow at first. This usually goes away after a week or two. Call your doctor if your heart beats very slowly, you feel very dizzy, or you cannot catch your breath.

Lisinopril:
This medicine lowers your blood pressure and helps your heart pump better. Take 10 mg once a day. You may get a dry cough. This is common and not dangerous. Your blood pressure should go down over the next week or two. Call your doctor if your face or lips swell, or if you feel dizzy when standing up.

Metformin:
This medicine helps control your blood sugar. Take 500 mg twice a day with your meals. Your stomach may feel upset or you may have loose stools at first. Eating with this medicine helps reduce these issues. These side effects usually get better in a few days. Call your doctor if you have severe stomach pain or if your stools stay very loose.
recovery_trajectory:
**Week 1:**
- You will feel tired and short of breath at first. This is normal.
- Rest most of the day. Walk slowly inside your home only.
- Use your inhaler exactly as your doctor prescribed. Do not skip doses.
- Do your breathing exercises with the incentive spirometer every 2 hours while awake.
- Cough up mucus into a tissue. Wash your hands after.
- Call your doctor if you cough up blood or rust-colored mucus.
- Your goal this week is to use your spirometer 8 times per day.

**Week 2:**
- You may have a little more energy than last week.
- Walk slowly for 5 to 10 minutes, two times per day.
- Keep using your inhalers on the same schedule as before.
- Do your breathing exercises every 2 hours. This helps clear your lungs.
- Drink plenty of water to help loosen mucus in your chest.
- Call your doctor if you feel more short of breath, not less.
- Your goal is to cough up less mucus each day.

**Week 3-4:**
- You should feel stronger. Shortness of breath should improve with rest.
- Slowly increase walking. Try 10 to 15 minutes, two times per day.
- Keep taking all your inhalers. Use them before you walk or exercise.
- Do your breathing exercises at least 4 times per day.
- Avoid smoke, dust, and cold air. These can trigger coughing.
- Go to your follow-up doctor visit. Bring a list of your medications.
- Call your doctor if you have a fever or yellow-green mucus.

**When to expect improvement:**
- Shortness of breath gets better slowly over several weeks.
- Keep your inhalers with you at all times.
- Do your breathing exercises every day. This is very important.
- Avoid people who are sick or coughing near you.
- Tell your doctor right away if you feel worse.
escalation_guide:
CALL 911 IMMEDIATELY
These symptoms are life-threatening. Do not drive yourself.
- Cannot breathe or gasping for air: Your lungs need help right now.
- Chest pain or pressure that will not go away: This can mean a heart problem.
- Blue lips or blue fingernails: Your body is not getting enough oxygen.
- Passing out or losing consciousness: Your brain needs oxygen right now.
- Coughing up blood: This is a sign of serious bleeding.
- Fast or very irregular heartbeat with dizziness: Your heart may not be pumping right.
- Signs of stroke like face drooping or arm weakness: Minutes matter for stroke treatment.

GO TO THE ER TODAY
Do not wait until tomorrow. Go within a few hours.
- Fever above 101 degrees F that will not go down: This can mean an infection.
- Coughing up yellow or green mucus: This can mean a lung infection.
- Wheezing that does not get better with your rescue inhaler: Your airways are blocked.
- Trouble speaking or swallowing: Your throat or airways may be swelling.
- Confusion or feeling very tired and weak: Your lungs may not be working well.
- Swelling in your legs or ankles: This can mean fluid is building up.

CALL YOUR DOCTOR
Call during office hours. Do not go to the ER for these.
- Mild cough that is slowly getting better: This is normal after treatment.
- Slight wheezing when you walk: This can happen during recovery from an attack.
- Questions about when to take your rescue inhaler: Your doctor will help you plan.
- Mild tiredness that is improving: Your body needs time to heal.
